source.title: Don't trust your eyes: on the (un)reliability of feature visualizations
source.authors: Robert Geirhos; R. Zimmermann; Blair Bilodeau; Wieland Brendel; Been Kim

record.tranche_reason: The paper uses a different, vision-model activation-similarity sanity check to assess whether feature visualizations explain how natural inputs are processed.
record.gate_note: The main empirical result compares activations from natural images and same-class feature visualizations across Inception-V1 layers. The text describes the broad layer-wise pattern, while exact plotted values are not supplied. Other results directly manipulate unit visualizations; they are recorded as findings about the subject but do not test a listed version. Results cited from other papers are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study does not test any version. Its empirical sanity check asks whether synthetic activation-maximization visualizations of last-layer Inception-V1 class units are processed like natural images. That is a different construct from V6, which concerns explanations fitted to a neuron's activating examples that then fail to predict where it fires. The authors state that highly activating natural images would pass their sanity check (App. A.3). The fooling experiments induce the misleading visualizations on purpose. The worst-case theory (argmax does not determine f) is related to V6 in spirit but involves no explanation scoring, firing-prediction rate or neuron-job share. These findings belong under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors also prove that activation-maximization visualizations are only guaranteed reliable under strong assumptions (e.g. low-dimensional affine functions). They recommend exploratory, not confirmatory, use of visualizations, and suggest building networks with enforced structure.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses vision-model feature visualizations and activation-similarity comparisons, rather than an audit of language-model neuron poles or automated held-out-text explanation scores.
record.method_sensitivity: The measured similarity pattern varied across network depth: it was low through roughly the first two thirds of layers and increased in the last third. The analysis used 10 selected classes and sampled comparisons rather than every possible comparison.

fits_no_version.finding: In the first two thirds of Inception-V1 layers, same-class feature visualizations are about as similar to natural images as different-class images are. Similarity rises in the last third. The result holds for Spearman, Pearson and cosine measures and is not explained by OOD shift (App. G).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Activation-maximization feature visualizations are processed along different paths than natural images of the class they represent.

fits_no_version.finding: Fooling circuits and silent units change visualizations arbitrarily with at most minimal accuracy change: Inception-V1 top-1 69.146% to 68.744%; ResNet-50 unchanged; robust ResNet50 63.924% to 63.784%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Feature visualizations can be manipulated without changing a model's behaviour on natural input.

fits_no_version.finding: Theory shows a unit's argmax/argmin cannot predict f(x), or even whether f(x) is nearer the max or min, for black-box, neural-network, piecewise-affine, monotone or convex functions. The authors say this extends to top-k activating dataset samples.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Maximally activating inputs alone cannot guarantee prediction of a unit's activation elsewhere.

record.peer_reviewed: International Conference on Machine Learning; Proceedings of Machine Learning Research, volume 235 (2024)
record.problems: The main activation-similarity analysis uses only 10 selected ImageNet classes and samples only some pairwise comparisons for Spearman and Pearson analyses. The paper reports plotted values rather than exact layer-wise numbers, and the shaded standard-deviation range is explicitly not a statistical-significance estimate. The authors also state that the tested architectures are not exhaustive.
record.rows_left_out: No additional result rows were left out.

untested.parts: No Qwen3-32B neuron-pole audit or job shares.
No language models, no MoE models, no scaling.
The cat-and-car neuron and the pose/recursive-generalization account are not examined.
No interpretable-neuron share across architectures or tools. Appendix D only correlates path linearity with human interpretability scores.
No attribution graphs and no replacement-model comparison.

No explanations written from activating examples and no held-out firing prediction. The sanity check concerns synthetic visualizations, which the authors say natural top-activating examples would pass.
No simulation-based scoring of explanations on new text.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V6 link conflates synthetic feature visualizations with explanations from activating examples. The study is vision-only (Inception-V1, ResNet-50). Appendix D (path linearity vs human interpretability, r=-.36) is preliminary and does not match V4's share-of-interpretable-neurons claim.

versions.untested_parts: The Qwen3-32B neuron-pole audit and its reported proportions are not studied.
No cross-model language-model audit, dense-versus-MoE comparison, or parameter scaling to trillions is performed.
The InceptionV1 cat-and-car example and the proposed shared-pose or recursive-generalization account are not tested.
The paper does not estimate the share of interpretable neurons under different architectures, regularization, or tools, or test the stated 5%-to-99% estimates.
Attribution graphs and whether a model's own neurons suffice as circuit units are not studied.

The study tests feature visualizations against natural-image activation patterns, not explanations written from activating examples followed by explicit held-out firing prediction for individual neurons.
The paper does not score neuron explanations by simulating their activations on new text or report the share of neurons achieving good automated scores.

rows.subject: Inception-V1
rows.operation_detail: Compared layer activations for natural images and same-class feature visualizations using normalized Spearman correlation.
rows.measure: Normalized similarity between activations for natural images and same-class feature visualizations across layers
rows.baseline: Normalized to natural images of the same class = 1 and natural images of different classes = 0
rows.value: The text reports that similarity through roughly the first two thirds of layers was about as low as similarity to unrelated-class images; exact values are figure-only.
rows.uncertainty: The plot's shaded region is described as a rough range extending two standard deviations; it is not a significance estimate.
rows.note: The paper interprets the low similarity as evidence that these visualizations do not reflect the processing of natural images in most of the network.
rows.check: Measures layer-wise activation similarity between same-class feature visualizations and natural images, not whether an explanation from activating examples predicts firing. It cannot show V6's effect. The value is figure-only.

rows.subject: Inception-V1
rows.operation_detail: Compared layer activations for natural images and same-class feature visualizations using normalized Spearman correlation.
rows.measure: Normalized similarity between activations for natural images and same-class feature visualizations across layers
rows.baseline: Normalized to natural images of the same class = 1 and natural images of different classes = 0
rows.value: The text says similarity increases in later layers; exact values are figure-only.
rows.uncertainty: The plot's shaded region is described as a rough range extending two standard deviations; it is not a significance estimate.
rows.note: The authors caution that higher late-layer correlation does not establish that the inputs follow the same processing paths.
rows.check: Same construct mismatch as r1. Rising late-layer similarity says nothing about explanation-based firing prediction. The value is figure-only.

rows.subject: Inception-V1
rows.operation_detail: Added a fooling circuit to make last-layer unit visualizations display unrelated or arbitrary patterns while retaining normal responses to natural input.

conditions.value: last-layer units; circuit replicated to permute visualizations or display arbitrary patterns

rows.measure: ImageNet validation top-1 and top-5 accuracy after manipulation
rows.note: This result concerns the effect of manipulating visualizations on classification accuracy, not the neuron-job proportions or held-out explanation prediction in the listed versions.
rows.check: Deliberately induced manipulation (fooling circuit). The accuracy values check that the manipulation preserved behaviour; they are not a measure of the phenomenon.

rows.subject: ResNet-50
rows.operation_detail: Added silent units to make visualizations for all 512 units in a selected layer near-identical.
rows.baseline: Unmanipulated layer visualizations; validation top-1 and top-5 accuracy
rows.value: Visualizations became near-identical; neither top-1 nor top-5 validation accuracy changed.
rows.note: The result demonstrates a constructed visualization manipulation, not a test of the listed neuron-job or held-out explanation-prediction claims.
rows.check: Deliberately induced silent-unit manipulation. This is a capability check, not a test.

rows.subject: ResNet50 (ℓ∞, ϵ = 4/255) by Salman et al. (2020)
rows.operation_detail: Applied the silent-unit method to make visualizations for all units in a selected layer near-identical.
rows.measure: Feature-visualization appearance and ImageNet validation top-1 accuracy
rows.note: This is an intentionally manipulated model and does not test a listed claim version.
rows.check: Deliberately induced manipulation on a robust ResNet50 (App. F). This is a capability check, not a test.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
